---
title: "Bash exercise using GitHub's codespace"
---

Follow the instructions below to complete this exercise, and put your answers
to the questions into the Exercise 2 quiz on Canvas.

## Your project repository

### Make your copy and open your codespace

1.  Go to the
    [Comp Bio project template](https://github.com/phyletica/comp-bio-project-template)
    on GitHub, and follow the instructions in its README under the following
    two sections **ONLY**:

    -   ***"Make your own copy of this repository"***:
        Name your repository **`bash-intro`**, and choose ***Public***
    -   ***"Open your codespace"***: When you get a "Do you trust the authors
        of the files in this folder?" pop-up, click "Trust Folder & Continue"

    Stop and come back here once you get to ***"Set up your project environment"***
    (don't set up the environment; we don't need it for this exercise).

2.  Once your codespace is ready, you should see your files on the left side
    of VS Code and a ***terminal*** at the bottom.
    Click in the terminal and check that you're in your project's folder:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pwd
    ls -a
    ```

    `pwd` (**p**rint **w**orking **d**irectory) tells you what directory
    ("folder") you are in, which should be `/workspaces/comp-bio-project`.
    This folder you are in is called your ***working directory***.
    `ls -a` lists all files and directories in your working directory. When you
    run this command, you should see `README.md` and a folder named
    `.devcontainer` (plus a folder named `.git`; more on that below).

The terminal is the Bash command line running on a Linux computer in the cloud.
All of the commands in this exercise are typed in the terminal.

## Creating a new directory and copying files into it

1.  Using the terminal, navigate to your home directory:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    cd ~
    ```

2.  Create a new directory called "exercise2"

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    mkdir exercise2
    ```

3.  Use the `curl` command to download an `answer1.txt` file from our class
    GitHub repo into your new `exercise2` directory:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    curl -L -o exercise2/answer1.txt https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phyletica/intro-to-comp-bio/refs/heads/main/notebooks/data/answer1.txt
    ```

4.  Use the `curl` command again to download the `SARS-CoV-2.fasta` file from
    our class GitHub repo into your new `exercise2` directory:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    curl -L -o exercise2/SARS-CoV-2.fasta https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phyletica/intro-to-comp-bio/refs/heads/main/notebooks/data/SARS-CoV-2.fasta
    ```

5.  Now, move into the "exercise2" directory and confirm the files you
    downloaded are there:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    cd exercise2
    ls
    ```

### Question 1

Use the command line (terminal) to see what is in the `answer1.txt` file.
Enter what you find in the file into Question 1 of the Exercise 2 quiz on
Canvas.

-   ***Hint***: The commands `cat` or `less` would be useful. I would normally
    encourage you to use the `man` command to learn more about these commands,
    but `man` doesn't work by default in GitHub's Codespaces.
    As an alternative, go to the
    [Linux man pages online](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/index.html)
    and use the search bar near the bottom of the page to search for the
    commands `cat` and `less`.

::: {.callout-important}
## Save your work to GitHub at the end of every part

Your GitHub codespace is ***temporary***.
It stops on its own after 30 minutes of inactivity, and GitHub ***deletes***
codespaces that haven't been used for 30 days, ***even if they contain work
you haven't pushed to GitHub***.
Your work is only safe once you have committed it and pushed it to GitHub
(you'll learn how in Part 1).
:::

## Manipulating sequence data

The "SARS-CoV-2.fasta" file contains nucleotide sequence data from different
strains of the SARS-CoV-2 virus.
The sequences are in a format called FASTA.
The FASTA format looks like:

    >Name1
    AATCGGCTA
    >Name2
    ATTCGCCTA

### Question 2

Use the command line to determine the number of sequences in the
"SARS-CoV-2.fasta" file.

-   Notice all sequences start with a ">" character to specify the seqence's
    name. We can use that to count the sequences efficiently. Try:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    grep ">" SARS-CoV-2.fasta
    ```

    NOTE: Putting quotes around the `>` character is important, because in the
    Bash language, this character is normally used to redirect output!

    `grep` is a very useful command for finding string patterns. You can learn
    more about it by searching for `grep` at the 
    [Linux man pages online](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/grep.1.html).

-   `grep` works okay for this small FASTA file, but what if there were 1000s
    of sequences in the file? You wouldn't want to count them "by hand!"

    We can use the `wc` command (***w***ord ***c***ount) for counting the
    sequences. Try:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    grep ">" SARS-CoV-2.fasta | wc -l
    ```

    The pipe (`|`) character converts, or "pipes", the output of one command to
    input to another command. `wc -l` will count the number of lines output by
    `grep`

Put the number of sequences into Question 2 of the Exercise 2 quiz on Canvas.
